planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container trees in spring once soil has warmed; Acco is an Israeli selection bred for an unusually early harvest, so it can extend the pomegranate season ahead of later main-crop cultivars.

directions: Acco is a compact, early-ripening pomegranate from Israel that reaches harvest well ahead of standard cultivars like Wonderful, making it useful for stretching out a home orchard's pomegranate season. Fruit is medium-sized with ruby-red skin, sweet flavor, and comparatively tender seeds, and the juice content of the arils tends to run higher than many other cultivars. Give it full sun and sharp drainage, since it is naturally suited to dry Mediterranean-type climates and appreciates good airflow in humid Gulf Coast summers to reduce fruit-skin blemishing. Once established it tolerates drought well and needs only occasional deep watering.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Pomegranates for Texas
California Rare Fruit Growers — Pomegranate Fruit Facts

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container trees in spring; Herskovitz is a small, early-ripening Israeli cultivar often grown alongside Acco and Wonderful in comparative pomegranate trials.

directions: Herskovitz is a small-fruited, early-season pomegranate from Israel commonly grown as a comparison cultivar alongside Acco and Wonderful in orchard trials. Its arils have a tangier, more tart-forward flavor than sweeter dessert cultivars and firmer seeds, which makes it a good choice for juicing or for gardeners who prefer a less cloying pomegranate. Plant in full sun with well-drained soil; the tree is naturally shrubby and compact, so it fits well in smaller Gulf Coast landscapes if given room to spread. Water deeply but infrequently once established, and thin crowded fruit clusters to improve size on the remaining fruit.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Pomegranates for Texas
California Rare Fruit Growers — Pomegranate Fruit Facts

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container trees in spring; Emek was registered in Israel in 2009 and ripens about six weeks ahead of Wonderful, giving Gulf Coast growers a very early pomegranate harvest.

directions: Emek is a vigorous, self-fertile Israeli pomegranate bred specifically for very early ripening, reaching harvest roughly six weeks before the widely grown Wonderful cultivar. Fruit is medium to large with an attractive dark pink to red skin and sweet, juicy red arils of good eating quality. Because it fruits so early, it can help a Gulf Coast garden get a jump on pomegranate season before summer humidity and fruit-splitting rains set in later on. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, and prune to an open vase shape to maximize airflow and light penetration into the fruiting wood.
sources: HortScience — 'Emek', a Red and Very Early-ripening New Pomegranate Cultivar
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Pomegranates for Texas

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container trees in late winter to early spring; Miss Kim was selected in the Southeast for its heat and humidity tolerance, a good match for Gulf Coast gardens.

directions: Miss Kim is a Southern-selected white mulberry valued for large, richly flavored, sweet berries and notably strong tolerance of heat and humidity, making it well adapted to Gulf Coast summers. Trees begin bearing within two to three years of planting and require little maintenance once established beyond an occasional shaping prune to keep the canopy at a manageable size. Give it full sun and average, well-drained soil; established trees tolerate drought well and need only supplemental water during prolonged dry spells. Because ripe fruit drops over an extended harvest window and can stain pavement, site it away from walkways, patios, and parked cars.
sources: Edible Landscaping — Miss Kim Mulberry
California Rare Fruit Growers — Mulberry Fruit Facts

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container trees in late winter to early spring in full sun; this is a large, vigorous tree that benefits from annual pruning if space is limited.

directions: White Ivory, a Whitman Farms selection, produces unusually large white berries with a light crimson blush and an intensely sweet, complex flavor that fans describe as among the best-tasting mulberries available. It grows into a substantial shade tree if left unpruned, so gardeners with smaller lots should plan on regular heading cuts to keep it at a manageable height. Its pale, non-staining fruit is especially good dried, and the extended ripening period spreads the harvest out over several weeks. Plant in full sun in average, well-drained soil, and expect a tough, low-maintenance tree once established.
sources: Edible Landscaping — White Ivory Mulberry
Burnt Ridge Nursery — White Ivory Mulberry

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container trees in late winter to early spring; Nikita ripens earlier than most white mulberries and stays naturally more compact than seedling trees.

directions: Nikita is a self-fertile white mulberry selection notable for ripening earlier than most other white-fruited cultivars, giving Gulf Coast gardeners an earlier start to the mulberry harvest. It stays naturally smaller and more compact than typical seedling mulberry trees, which makes it a better fit for home landscapes with limited space. Fruit is large, juicy, and very sweet, and the tree shows good resistance to pests along with solid drought tolerance once established. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, and expect fruiting to begin at a young age with minimal care required beyond occasional pruning.
sources: Edible Landscaping — Nikita White Mulberry
California Rare Fruit Growers — Mulberry Fruit Facts

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container trees in late winter to early spring; Paradise stays compact at around 15 feet, making it a good choice for smaller Gulf Coast yards.

directions: Paradise is a thornless, self-fertile mulberry that stays a compact, broad-canopied small tree rather than growing into the large shade tree many mulberry seedlings become, making it easier to manage and harvest in a home garden. Fruit is ivory-colored with a light purple blush at full ripeness, medium-sized, and very sweet, ripening in the early-to-mid part of the mulberry season. It handles heat and humidity exceptionally well and tolerates drought once established, though it should be sited with some protection from deer browsing, since young growth is palatable. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil for the heaviest fruit set.
sources: Edible Landscaping — Paradise Mulberry
California Rare Fruit Growers — Mulberry Fruit Facts

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container trees in late winter to early spring; this selection is more cold-hardy than black-fruited mulberries and well suited to Gulf Coast heat.

directions: White Pakistan produces strikingly long, creamy white berries that commonly stretch three to five inches, with a rich, honey-like sweetness and very little acidity that makes them excellent for fresh eating straight off the tree. It is a distinct, alba-type selection from the better-known Morus macroura 'Pakistan' shahtoot, and is noted for being more cold-hardy than black-fruited mulberry cultivars while retaining strong heat tolerance for Gulf Coast summers. The tree grows vigorously into an ornamental, productive landscape specimen with a long harvest window. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, and prune as needed to keep the long fruit clusters within easy reach.
sources: Edible Landscaping — White Pakistan Mulberry
California Rare Fruit Growers — Mulberry Fruit Facts

planting.note: Plant bare-root or containerized trees in late winter to early spring; UFQueen has an unusually low chill requirement near 250 hours, an excellent match for warm Gulf Coast winters.

directions: UFQueen is a University of Florida-bred nectarine selected from among about eighty seedlings for its very low chilling requirement of roughly 250 hours, making it one of the earliest and most reliably fruitful nectarines for mild-winter Gulf Coast gardens. Fruit ripens quite early in the season and has firm, non-melting yellow flesh under red-blushed skin, giving good handling and shelf life compared to soft melting-flesh types. Give it full sun and well-drained soil, and be prepared for the smooth skin to need extra attention to thinning and pest management, since nectarines are more susceptible to fruit-boring insects than fuzzy-skinned peaches in humid climates. Prune annually to an open center to maintain good light penetration and airflow.
sources: U.S. Plant Patent PP11587 — Nectarine tree named 'UFQueen'
UF/IFAS EDIS Circular 1159 — Florida Peach and Nectarine Varieties

planting.note: Plant bare-root or containerized trees in late winter to early spring; GulfAtlas was released in 2014 by the joint UF/UGA/USDA-ARS Gulf series peach breeding program with a roughly 400 chill unit requirement.

directions: GulfAtlas is the latest-ripening member of the Gulf series of peaches jointly released by the University of Florida, University of Georgia, and USDA-ARS Byron program, reaching harvest about three weeks after its sibling Gulfcrimson in mid-June. It bears very large, round, non-melting clingstone fruit with bright yellow flesh and heavy red blush over yellow ground color, giving growers a way to extend the low-chill peach harvest later into the season than most Gulf Coast cultivars. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, and expect a moderate chill requirement of around 400 hours, higher than the earliest Gulf series releases but still workable in much of the Gulf Coast. Thin fruit to improve size and prune annually to an open vase form for good light penetration into the fruiting wood.
sources: USDA ARS — Gulfprince and Gulfcrest Peaches Released (Gulf series program history)
UF/IFAS North Florida Research and Education Center — New Peach Cultivar Trial
